text: Ariane 5, a retired European heavy-lift space launch vehicle operated by Arianespace for the European Space Agency (ESA), was launched from the Guiana Space Centre (CSG) in French Guiana and was used to deliver payloads into geostationary transfer orbit (GTO), low Earth orbit (LEO), or further into space. It achieved a streak of 82 consecutive successful launches between 9 April 2003 and 12 December 2017. Developed by the Centre National d'Études Spatiales (CNES) in cooperation with various European partners, it was designed as an expendable launch vehicle and classified as part of the Ariane rocket family. Aérospatiale, and later ArianeGroup, served as the prime contractor, leading a multi-country consortium. Originally intended to launch the Hermes spacecraft, Ariane 5 was rated for human space launches. The vehicle evolved through successive versions: "G", "G+", "GS", "ECA", and finally "ES". It featured a dual-launch capability using a SYLDA (Système de Lancement Double Ariane) carrier system to mount up to two large geostationary belt communication satellites, and a SPELTRA (Structure Porteuse Externe Lancement Triple Ariane) system to carry up to three smaller main satellites, with an ASAP (Ariane Structure for Auxiliary Payloads) platform enabling up to eight secondary payloads. The cryogenic H173 main stage (H158 for Ariane 5G, G+, and GS) consisted of a 5.4 m (18 ft) diameter by 30.5 m (100 ft) high tank with two compartments—one for liquid oxygen and one for liquid hydrogen—powered by a Vulcain 2 engine with a vacuum thrust of 1,390 kN (310,000 lbf); the H173 EPC weighed about 189 t (417,000 lb), including 175 t (386,000 lb) of propellant, and re-entered the atmosphere for an ocean splashdown. Two P241 (P238 for Ariane 5G and G+) solid rocket boosters (SRBs or EAPs from the French Étages d'Accélération à Poudre) were attached to the sides, each weighing about 277 t (611,000 lb) full and delivering a thrust of about 7,080 kN (1,590,000 lbf), fueled by a mix of ammonium perchlorate (68%), aluminium fuel (18%), and HTPB (14%), burning for 130 seconds before being dropped into the ocean; they were usually allowed to sink but could be recovered with parachutes for post-flight analysis, though not reused, with the most recent recovery occurring in 2009 for the first Ariane 5 ECA mission. The French M51 submarine-launched ballistic missile (SLBM) shared substantial technology with these boosters. In February 2000, a suspected nose cone of an Ariane 5 booster was recovered by beachcombers on the South Texas coast before government intervention. The second stage, originally the EPS (Étage à Propergols Stockables) using monomethylhydrazine and nitrogen tetroxide with 10,000 kg (22,000 lb) of storable propellant, was improved for use on Ariane 5G+, GS, and ES, and demonstrated repeated ignition during flight V26 on 5 October 2007, with the first operational use occurring on 9 March 2008 for the Automated Transfer Vehicle (ATV) mission, involving three burns. The Ariane 5ECA used the ESC (Étage Supérieur Cryotechnique), fueled by liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen, with the HM7B engine previously used in the Ariane 4 third stage, providing 6.5 tonne of thrust and burning for 945 seconds, with hydrogen gas thrusters for roll control during powered flight and full attitude control during payload separation, and oxygen gas thrusters for longitudinal acceleration after engine cutoff. The payload and upper stages were protected by a fairing made by Ruag Space, jettisoned above 100 km (62 mi; 54 nmi), and composed of four panels from flight VA-238 onward. Components were assembled in Europe and shipped to French Guiana by boat, then assembled in the Launcher Integration Building (BIL), transferred to the Final Assembly Building (BAF) for payload and fairing mating, and finally moved to the Launch Zone (ZL) for fueling and launch. As of November 2014, the commercial launch price for a midsize satellite in the lower position was approximately €50 million, with the heavier satellite in the upper position priced at about €90 million as of 2013, and the total launch price for two satellites to space, one in the upper and one in the lower position, around €150 million as of January 2015. The Ariane 5 ME (Mid-life Evolution), in development into early 2015, was intended as a stopgap between Ariane 5ECA/Ariane 5ES and Ariane 6, with a first flight planned for 2018, and was to use a new upper stage with increased propellant volume powered by the Vinci engine, capable of multiple restarts for complex orbital maneuvers, including direct insertion into geosynchronous orbit, planetary exploration, and guaranteed upper stage deorbiting or graveyard orbit, with a lengthened fairing up to 20 m (66 ft), a new dual launch system, and a 15% increase in payload to GTO to 11,500 kg (25,400 lb), projected to reduce cost-per-kilogram by 20%. Originally known as Ariane 5ECB, development was canceled in 2003 due to the failure of the first ECA flight in 2002 and a deteriorating satellite industry, though development of the Vinci engine continued. In 2009, EADS Astrium received a €200 million contract and on 10 April 2012 another €112 million to continue development, with total effort expected to cost €1 billion. On 21 November 2012, ESA agreed to continue with Ariane 5ME to meet lower-priced competitors, with the Vinci upper stage also to be used as the second stage of Ariane 6 and further commonality sought. The qualification flight was scheduled for mid-2018, followed by gradual introduction into service. On 2 December 2014, ESA decided to halt funding for Ariane 5ME and focus on Ariane 6, which was expected to have a lower cost per launch and greater payload flexibility using two or four P120C solid boosters depending on total payload mass. Work on the Ariane 5 EAP motors continued in the Vega programme, with the Vega 1st stage engine—the P80—being a shorter derivation of the EAP, featuring a filament wound graphite epoxy casing, a new composite steerable nozzle, improved thermal insulation, a narrower throat, and electromechanical actuators replacing hydraulic ones for thrust vector control. These developments might have been incorporated into the Ariane programme, though likely based on early blueprints of Ariane 6 featuring a central P80 booster and 2–4 around it; a design incorporating the ESC-B, improved solid motor casing, and an uprated Vulcain engine would have delivered 27,000 kg (60,000 lb) to LEO, intended for lunar missions but potentially constrained by high Max-Q for launch mass. The design brief for Ariane 6 called for a lower-cost and smaller launch vehicle capable of launching a single satellite of up to 6,500 kg (14,300 lb) to GTO, though the finalized design was nearly identical in performance to Ariane 5, focusing instead on lowering fabrication costs and launch prices, with a projected cost of about €70 million per flight as of March 2014—about half of Ariane 5's price. Initial development was projected to cost €3.6 billion, with ESA setting 16 July 2020 as the deadline for the first flight; the Ariane 6 successfully completed its maiden flight on 9 July 2024. Ariane 5's first test flight (Flight 501) on 4 June 1996 failed due to a software malfunction in the control system, where a 64-bit floating-point value was incorrectly converted to a 16-bit signed integer, causing a processor trap because the value exceeded the 16-bit range; the software, written in Ada, was reused from the Ariane 4 despite not being required by Ariane 5 due to different preparation sequences, with three variables, including horizontal bias, unprotected due to perceived safety margins. The second test flight (L502, 30 October 1997) was a partial failure due to a Vulcain nozzle roll problem leading to premature core stage shutdown; the third test flight (L503, 21 October 1998) was successful, and the first commercial launch (L504) occurred on 10 December 1999 with the XMM-Newton satellite. A partial failure occurred on 12 July 2001, delivering two satellites into only half the intended GTO height; the ESA Artemis satellite reached its intended orbit on 31 January 2003 via ion propulsion. The next launch was on 1 March 2002, successfully placing the Envisat satellite into an 800 km (500 mi) orbit, the heaviest single payload until the first ATV launch on 9 March 2008. The first ECA launch on 11 December 2002 failed due to a coolant pipe leak causing nozzle overheating, resulting in a self-destruct three minutes into flight and loss of two satellites (STENTOR and Hot Bird 7) valued at about €630 million; this failure delayed the Rosetta mission from January 2003 to 26 February 2004, then to early March 2004 due to a foam fault. This was the last Ariane 5 failure until flight 241 in January 2018. On 27 September 2003, the last Ariane 5G flight (Flight 162) boosted three satellites, including the first European lunar probe SMART-1. On 18 July 2004, an Ariane 5G+ launched the heaviest telecommunications satellite at the time, Anik F2, weighing almost 6,000 kg (13,000 lb). The first successful Ariane 5ECA launch occurred on 12 February 2005, carrying the XTAR-EUR military satellite, a 'SLOSHSAT' small scientific satellite, and a MaqSat B2 payload simulator, delayed from October 2004 due to testing and a prior military launch. On 11 August 2005, the first Ariane 5GS (featuring improved solid motors) launched Thaicom 4, the heaviest telecommunications satellite at 6,505 kg (14,341 lb). On 16 November 2005, the third Ariane 5ECA launch (second successful ECA) carried a dual payload of Spaceway F2 for DirecTV and Telkom-2 for PT Telekomunikasi of Indonesia, the heaviest dual payload at over 8,000 kg (18,000 lb).

On 12 February 2005, an Ariane 5 launch carried the XTAR-EUR military communications satellite, the 'SLOSHSAT' small scientific satellite, and a MaqSat B2 payload simulator; the launch had been originally scheduled for October 2004 but was delayed due to additional testing and a prior military launch of a Helios 2A observation satellite. On 11 August 2005, the first Ariane 5GS, equipped with improved solid motors from the Ariane 5ECA, launched Thaicom 4, the heaviest telecommunications satellite at 6,505 kg (14,341 lb), into orbit. On 16 November 2005, the third Ariane 5ECA launch—its second successful ECA flight—carried a dual payload of Spaceway F2 for DirecTV and Telkom-2 for PT Telekomunikasi of Indonesia, marking the vehicle's heaviest dual payload to date at over 8,000 kg (18,000 lb). On 27 May 2006, an Ariane 5ECA set a new commercial payload record of 8,200 kg (18,100 lb) with the dual payload of Thaicom 5 and Satmex 6. On 4 May 2007, the Ariane 5ECA lifted Astra 1L and Galaxy 17 into transfer orbit with a combined weight of 8,600 kg (19,000 lb) and a total payload of 9,400 kg (20,700 lb), a record later surpassed by the November 2007 launch of Skynet 5B and Star One C1, which achieved a total payload of 9,535 kg (21,021 lb). On 9 March 2008, the first Ariane 5ES-ATV was launched to deliver the Jules Verne ATV to the International Space Station, the heaviest payload ever launched by a European vehicle, providing propellant, water, air, and dry cargo; this mission was the first operational Ariane flight with an engine restart in the upper stage, using the restartable ES-ATV Aestus EPS upper stage. On 1 July 2009, an Ariane 5ECA launched TerreStar-1 (now EchoStar T1), weighing 6,910 kg (15,230 lb) at the time the largest and most massive commercial telecommunication satellite ever built, until surpassed by Telstar 19 Vantage at 7,080 kg (15,610 lb) launched on Falcon 9; it was placed into a lower-energy orbit with an initial apogee of roughly 17,900 km (11,100 mi). On 28 October 2010, an Ariane 5ECA launched Eutelsat's W3B and B-SAT's BSAT-3b; the W3B failed shortly after launch due to an oxidizer leak in its main propulsion system and was declared a total loss, while BSAT-3b operates normally. On 15 August 2020, the VA253 launch introduced minor improvements—lighter avionics and guidance-equipment bay and modified pressure vents on the payload fairing—that increased lift capacity by about 85 kg (187 lb), necessary for the James Webb Space Telescope launch, and also featured a Galileo navigation satellite location system. On 25 December 2021, VA256 launched the James Webb Space Telescope toward a Sun–Earth L2 halo orbit; the precise trajectory led to fuel savings that potentially doubled the telescope’s lifetime by preserving more hydrazine propellant, and the flight used components that had performed well in pre-flight testing, including 'one of the best Vulcain engines ever built.' On 22 April 2011, VA-201 broke a commercial record by lifting Yahsat 1A and Intelsat New Dawn to transfer orbit with a total payload of 10,064 kg (22,187 lb), later surpassed by VA-208 on 2 August 2012 with 10,182 kg (22,447 lb), and again by VA-212 six months later with 10,317 kg (22,745 lb) sent to geosynchronous transfer orbit. In June 2016, the GTO record was raised to 10,730 kg (23,660 lb), the first rocket to carry a satellite dedicated to financial institutions, later increased by 5 kg (11 lb) to 10,735 kg (23,667 lb) on 24 August 2016 with Intelsat 33e and Intelsat 36; on 1 June 2017, the record was broken to 10,865 kg (23,953 lb) with ViaSat-2 and Eutelsat-172B; in 2021, VA-255 placed 11,210 kg into GTO. On 25 January 2018, an Ariane 5ECA launched SES-14 and Al Yah 3; about 9 minutes and 28 seconds after launch, a telemetry loss occurred, but both satellites were confirmed successfully separated and in contact with ground controllers, though their orbital inclinations were incorrect due to compromised guidance systems; as a result, both conducted orbital procedures, extending commissioning times—SES-14 required about 8 weeks longer than planned, entering service in early September instead of July, while Al Yah 3, after over 12 hours without further updates, was confirmed healthy and its maneuvering plan revised; by 16 February 2018, Al Yah 3 was approaching its intended geostationary orbit after recovery maneuvers; the investigation found that invalid inertial units' azimuth values had sent the vehicle 17° off course but to the correct altitude, as the guidance systems were programmed for a 90° standard geostationary transfer orbit when a 70° supersynchronous transfer orbit was intended, resulting in a 20° deviation; this anomaly ended the 82 consecutive launch success streak from 2003. Ariane 5 had accumulated 117 launches, 112 of which were successful, yielding a 95.7% success rate, with 83 consecutive missions without failure between April 2003 and December 2017, followed by a partial failure in January 2018. All launches occurred from the Guiana Space Centre, ELA-3.
